findings.description: In `scheduleTask`, any non-number return from the native set function is treated as an object handle, so `isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)` is evaluated on it. Some polyfills and environments return `undefined` or `null` from `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` or `requestAnimationFrame`. The old code explicitly guarded against this. For those environments the new code throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'refresh')` while scheduling, which is a regression.

If the native set function returns null or undefined (some polyfills, mocks or browsers do this, and the old code explicitly allowed it), `isNumber` is false and the code reads `handleOrId.refresh`. That throws a TypeError, so scheduling a timer, rAF or immediate crashes where it previously worked and returned the task. The access needs a null guard.

The checks `if (handleId)` and `if (handleId)` in the scheduling path replaced `typeof handle === 'number'`. A numeric handle of 0 is now treated as missing, so it is never stored in `tasksByHandleId`, the task is never cleaned up and `clearTimeout(0)` cannot cancel it. The code then falls through to return `handle ?? handleId ?? task`.

The pseudo-function handling assumes any selector part starting with `:where(` or `:is(` ends with the matching `)`, and drops the last character with `slice(prefix.length, -1)`. Parts like `:is(.a):hover`, `:where(.x).active` or `:is(.a, .b).foo` have a suffix after the closing paren. The final character of the suffix gets chopped, and the remaining `)` and suffix are then scoped as if they were inner selector content. The generated CSS is corrupted, for example `:is(.a):hover` becomes `:is(.a):hove)`. The `:where(a):where(b)` test only passes because of this same quirk.

The code assumes any part that starts with `:where(` or `:is(` also ends with the matching `)`, and unwraps it with `selectorPart.slice(prefix.length, -1)`. A compound part such as `:is(.a):hover`, `:where(.a).b` or `:is(.a)::before` doesn't end in `)`. In that case the slice drops the last character of the trailing text and mangles the inner selector. The output is then wrapped with a fixed `)`, which produces invalid CSS (for example the trailing `r` of `:hover` is lost). These are common selectors, so this is a regression for existing users.

The afterRenderEffect reads `componentExplorerView()` and calls `init()` on every update. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` message-bus listener, so listeners pile up and leak. Each run also recreates both InjectorTreeVisualizer instances, which resets zoom, pan and the rendered graph on every forest update. Previously the listeners and setup ran once, in `afterNextRender`.

The template still passes the raw `providers()` input to `ng-injector-providers`. The new `sortedProviders` computed is never used. Providers were previously sorted by token before display, so the list now appears unsorted, which is a regression.

Visibility is now toggled with the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements instead of a `display: none` class. The native `hidden` attribute is overridden by any author CSS `display` rule, such as a `:host { display: block/flex }` rule on these components. Inactive tabs may therefore stay visible and overlap. The old `ng-injector-tree.hidden` workaround (visibility hidden, absolutely positioned) was also removed, so a hidden injector tree may be laid out with zero size for the d3 visualizer.

The afterRenderEffect write callback reads componentExplorerView() and diDebugAPIsAvailable(), so it re-runs on every new view. Each run calls init(), which registers another 'highlightComponent' message-bus listener, so handlers pile up and fire multiple times per event. It also calls setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer() and setUpElementInjectorVisualizer() each time. That rebuilds both visualizers on every component tree update and discards zoom/pan state. Previously init() ran once.

The template still passes providers() to ng-injector-providers, but the sorting moved into the new sortedProviders computed, which nothing uses. The provider list is now shown unsorted, which regresses the previous token-sorted order.

Tab visibility now uses the [hidden] attribute instead of the removed .hidden CSS class. The native hidden attribute is `display:none` from the user-agent stylesheet, so any component whose host sets `display: block/flex` overrides it and the tab stays visible. The old special case for ng-injector-tree (visibility:hidden, position:absolute) is also gone. The injector tree now lays out and updates its d3 graphs under display:none, where size measurements can be zero.

The zone.js dependency moves from the `@npm//` external repo to the root-repo target `//:node_modules/zone.js`. `pkg_web` places files from the two sources at different paths (`npm/node_modules/...` versus `node_modules/...`). The matching `index.html` for this devapp is not updated in the diff, though the demo-standalone one is. If it still loads `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`, the script returns a 404 and the app starts without zone.js. Removing `tslib.js` from the package is also unverified for any HTML or non-bundled consumers.

The zone.js source changes to `//:node_modules/zone.js`, which changes where it lands in the packaged output. The shell-browser `index.html` and any manifest or packaging rules are not updated in the diff. If they still reference the old `npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` path, the extension shell fails to load zone.js.

The zone.js source changed from `@npm//:node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` (served under `npm/node_modules/...`) to the `//:node_modules/zone.js` package target. The package is now served at a different path, `node_modules/zone.js/...`. The matching `devtools/src/index.html` is not updated in this diff, so it probably still points at `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`. If it does, the dev app will 404 on zone.js and fail to bootstrap. The demo-standalone `index.html` was updated for this path change, but this one was not.

The zone.js file was replaced with the `//:node_modules/zone.js` package target, which changes where it lands in the output tree. The shell-browser `index.html` is not updated in this diff. If it still references `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`, the extension's pages will fail to load zone.js.

`get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever the name contains `__`, but the preceding loop also accepts non-field attributes on related objects, such as a property or method result like `parent__some_property`. For those, `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`. Neither is caught, so the changelist crashes where it previously rendered the value. The same happens for a name like `parent__is_active__foo`.

`f` is now the related model's final field, but `items_for_result` still treats it as a field of the row object. If the final field is a ForeignKey (for example `parent__parent`), the code runs `getattr(result, f.name)` on the wrong model. This raises `AttributeError` or shows the wrong value, instead of using the traversed value. Fields with choices or other formatting also go through `display_for_field` with a value taken from a different path. This changes behavior beyond boolean icons.

`lookup_field` now sets `f` to the final field of a `__` path, but `items_for_result` assumes `f` is a field on the row's own model. If the final field is a ForeignKey (e.g. `parent__some_fk`), `f.remote_field` is a ManyToOneRel and the code calls `getattr(result, f.name)`. That attribute doesn't exist on the row model, so it raises AttributeError or returns the wrong object. This used to render the related object's string. It is a regression for any related FK in `list_display`.

`get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever `LOOKUP_SEP` is in `name`, without catching FieldDoesNotExist. The attribute-walking loop above accepts any attribute, such as a property or method on the related object, or a reverse accessor. The extra field lookup then raises FieldDoesNotExist and crashes the changelist or readonly rendering. The old code returned a value for these cases.

Search terms for non-text `__exact` lookups are validated with `formfield().to_python()`. For a non-null `BooleanField`, forms.BooleanField.to_python turns any string other than 'false', '0' or 'False' into True, so it never raises ValidationError. A search for 'foo' on `bool__exact` therefore becomes `bool=True` and matches every True row. Before this change, the Cast-to-string lookup would not match them. Form-field coercion can also give unexpected results for relation fields. `ModelChoiceField.to_python` runs a DB query per term and applies `limit_choices_to`, and it passes a model instance as the lookup value.

Validation relies on `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. For fields with `choices`, `formfield()` returns a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python` just returns a string and does no type coercion or validation. For an `IntegerField(choices=...)` or similar in an `__exact` search, a term like "foo" is therefore not skipped. The raw string is passed to the lookup, and `get_prep_value` raises `ValueError` ("Field expected a number but got 'foo'"), so the admin changelist crashes. This reintroduces the crash that #26001 originally fixed. Validating with the model field's `to_python`/`get_prep_value`, or catching `ValueError`, would avoid it.

The new `wrap()` loses blank lines and trailing newlines. It iterates `text.splitlines(True)` and calls `TextWrapper.wrap()` on each line. `TextWrapper` replaces whitespace (including `
`) with spaces and drops trailing whitespace, so a line that is only `"
"` or empty wraps to `[]` and is dropped. For example, `"a

b"` becomes `"a
b"`, which removes paragraph breaks. Text ending in `"
"` loses the trailing newline, because the final `"
".join(result)` adds none. This regresses the old behaviour and the existing `wordwrap` tests that preserve newlines. The fix is to use `splitlines()` without keepends and append `""` to the result when `text.endswith("
")`.

The rewrite of wrap() with textwrap.TextWrapper regresses newline handling. Each line from splitlines(True) is wrapped separately and the results are joined with '
'. For a blank or whitespace-only line, TextWrapper.wrap() returns [] because the whitespace is dropped, so blank lines and paragraph breaks vanish. A trailing newline on the text is also lost. For example, 'a

b' becomes 'a
b', and 'text
' becomes 'text'. The old implementation preserved these. This changes the output of the wordwrap filter for multi-paragraph text. Empty or whitespace-only lines need to be restored, and a trailing newline preserved.

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals. For a constant such as `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ "a..b" }}`, FilterExpression sets `.var` to the resolved string rather than a Variable. The deprecation warning then fires for a valid literal that has no double-dot lookup. Under the planned error elevation, valid templates would fail to compile. The check should apply only when `.var` is a `Variable` that is a lookup, not a literal.

The warning message reads `self.origin.name`, but `Parser.origin` defaults to None when a Parser is built without an origin. Parsing a variable containing `..` would then raise AttributeError instead of emitting a warning.

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals. For a constant such as `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ _("Wait..") }}`, FilterExpression resolves `.var` to the plain string content. Any literal containing `..` (including an ellipsis `...`) therefore triggers the double-dot lookup deprecation warning, even though no variable lookup is involved. This is a false positive. It would also become a spurious TemplateSyntaxError once the deprecation ends. The check should only apply to Variable objects that perform lookups, i.e. when `var` is a Variable with no literal and a non-empty `lookups`.

The prefetch filter now builds ColPairs with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias, instead of resolving the field through the query. The generated SQL therefore always references the model's own table by name. This breaks when the target fields live on a parent table (multi-table inheritance), because the columns are qualified with the child's table. It also breaks when the base table alias differs from the table name, for example a custom prefetch queryset that was already aliased. The result is a wrong-column or missing-table error, or wrong rows. The old `field__in` path resolved the field correctly through the ORM.

The join-less single-column `field__in` optimization is removed, so every ordinary single-column FK prefetch now goes through the composite-key `TupleIn` path. This produces a row-value style `(col) IN ((v1),(v2))` clause. Some backends handle that poorly, and it can hurt index usage or hit parameter limits. Null FK values such as `(None,)` are also now passed raw into the tuple lookup, where the old code relied on the `In` lookup to strip them. This is a regression risk for the most common prefetch case.

`writer="html"` replaces `writer_name="html"`. Before docutils 0.22, `publish_parts` expects `writer` to be a Writer instance and takes names only through `writer_name`. With an older docutils, the string is treated as the writer object and `Publisher.set_components` skips the name lookup because `writer` is not None. `parse_rst` then fails with an AttributeError such as `'str' object has no attribute 'write'` or `'translate'`. This breaks every admindocs page that renders RST (views, models, template tags and filters) for users on docutils versions that Django still supports.

`writer="html"` passes a string to the `writer` parameter of `publish_parts`. Only docutils 0.22+ accepts a name there. In older docutils, `writer` must be a Writer instance, and `writer_name` is the parameter that takes a name. On those versions the string is used as the writer object and `parse_rst` will probably raise (for example an AttributeError), which would break admindocs. The change drops `writer_name` without a version check or fallback, so it breaks compatibility with older supported docutils.

The help tooltip spans lose their `title` attribute and get `aria-label` instead. A `span` has no role, so `aria-label` on it is generally ignored by assistive technology. Sighted users no longer get the hover tooltip, so the explanation of the filter input is no longer reliably exposed to anyone. The same applies to the selected-filter span.

The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields (e.g. `fields=['-name']`). `_check_local_fields` therefore reports a false 'refers to the nonexistent field "-name"' error (models.E012) for valid descending indexes. The old code used `fields_orders`, which strips the prefix. Building a set also makes the order of reported errors nondeterministic.

W037 checks `any(self.condition is not None for index in model._meta.indexes)`, so the generator ignores `index` and tests `self.condition`. If the current index has a condition, the warning is emitted for all indexes. If another index on the model has a condition but this one doesn't, no warning is emitted for that other index's own turn... it is only emitted when it is itself checked, which is fine, but the expression is plainly wrong. The W040 and W043 checks have a related fault: they scan every index on the model from inside a per-index method, so a model with N indexes gets the same warning N times, and indexes that don't use the feature still trigger it.

All index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop and are skipped when no database is routable or `databases` is empty/None. Name checks (E033/E034) and field-reference checks (E012 etc.) are no longer run in those cases, which is a regression. With multiple databases, every error is duplicated once per database. The tests had to be changed to pass `databases=self.databases` to keep passing.

The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix for descending indexes (e.g. `fields=['-name']`). The old code used `fields_orders`, which has the prefix stripped. `_check_local_fields` will now report a false 'nonexistent field' error (models.E012) for every valid descending index. It should use the stripped names from `fields_orders`.

The index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop, behind `allow_migrate_model`. The name checks (E033/E034) and the field-reference checks (E012 and similar) are no longer run when `databases` is empty or no database allows migrating the model. With several databases they are reported once per database. Previously they ran once, unconditionally. The tests were changed to pass `databases=self.databases`, which hides this regression.

The feature checks in `Index.check` still iterate over all `model._meta.indexes`. W040 and W043 fire for every index on the model if any one index uses `include` or expressions. W037 uses `self.condition` inside a generator over `index`, so it ignores `index` entirely. Since `check` is now called once per index, a model with several indexes gets duplicate warnings, and an index without `include` or expressions gets a warning meant for another index. Each check should look only at `self`.

The code now reads `window.relatedWindows`, but in this file `relatedWindows` is, as far as I recall, a block-scoped `const` inside the IIFE-style block, and nothing in the diff shows it being assigned to `window`. In production, `window.relatedWindows` would be `undefined`, so `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` would throw a TypeError. `win.close()` would never run, and the popup would stay open after the user selects an object. The new test hides this because its `beforeEach` sets `window.relatedWindows = []` itself, so it does not exercise the real code path. The other places that push to or splice `relatedWindows` still use the local variable, so they would be inconsistent with this change.

The code now reads `window.relatedWindows`, but in this file `relatedWindows` appears to be a module-local `const` inside the IIFE and is never assigned to `window`. If so, `window.relatedWindows` is undefined in production, so `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` throws a TypeError. The throw happens before `win.close()`, so a raw-id lookup popup would never close after the user selects a value. The new test hides this by setting `window.relatedWindows = window.relatedWindows || []` itself.

In the insert path, `returning_fields.append(field)` runs unconditionally whenever the value has `resolve_expression`. A field with `db_returning=True` (for example a `db_default` field left unset, whose value is a `DatabaseDefault` expression, or one assigned an expression) is already in `meta.db_returning_fields`. It is therefore appended a second time, so the same column appears twice in the RETURNING clause. This can break the INSERT on backends that reject duplicate returning columns. It also makes `_assign_returned_values` set the attribute twice, and it can misalign values with fields. The fix is to append only if `field not in returning_fields`.

In the insert path, if a field with db_returning=True (already in meta.db_returning_fields) is assigned an expression, it is appended to returning_fields a second time. The RETURNING clause then contains the column twice, and the field's value is assigned twice from duplicate returned values. The append needs a `field not in returning_fields` guard.

The `elif field.db_returning: returning_fields.remove(field)` branch runs on every backend. On backends without can_return_columns_from_insert (MySQL/MariaDB), if the pk is explicitly set and another field is assigned an expression, the auto field is removed from returning_fields but the expression field is appended. The compiler's non-RETURNING path then returns last_insert_id as a single value, and _assign_returned_values zips it with the first returning field. That puts the lastrowid into the expression field instead of deferring it, so the field gets a wrong value. The removal must be restricted to backends that can return columns and must skip the auto field when the pk is set.

get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for over-long codes, but callers that pass untrusted input only catch LookupError. get_language_from_request() passes the unbounded language cookie, and get_language_from_path() passes a regex-matched path prefix of arbitrary length. A request with a cookie over 500 characters, or a path like /xxxx.../, that has no '-' before the limit (or a strict lookup) raises an uncaught ValueError. LocaleMiddleware then returns a 500 error, a regression for requests that used to fall back to the default language.

get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for codes over 500 characters, but callers only catch LookupError. get_language_from_path() passes a regex-matched URL prefix of unbounded length, and LocaleMiddleware and i18n_patterns resolve through it. A request path like /xxxx…(>500 chars)/ now raises an unhandled ValueError, which produces a 500 error instead of a normal 404 or fallback. This is a regression of existing behavior.

The cast type is built from `field.db_type()` rather than a cast-safe type (`cast_db_type`). For AutoField, BigAutoField and SmallAutoField, `db_type` is `serial`, `bigserial` or `smallserial`. These are pseudo-types and cannot be used in a cast, so `(%s)::serial[]` is a PostgreSQL syntax error. Any `bulk_create` of 2 or more objects with explicit primary keys on an auto field will now crash. That path is common, for example when pks are supplied or a fixture is loaded. The `endswith('[]')` check does not catch this case.

The UNNEST path discards per-field placeholders (`field.get_placeholder`) and any other field-specific SQL wrapping. It builds the casts purely from `db_type`. Fields that rely on custom placeholders, such as geometry fields or custom fields, will be inserted incorrectly or fail. Fields whose `db_type` is None or non-castable are also not excluded.

The cast type is built with `field.db_type(connection)` instead of `cast_db_type()`. For a `CharField` with `max_length=None`, which PostgreSQL supports, the cast can come out as an invalid type such as `varchar(None)`. `cast_db_type` is the method that handles this case. `bulk_create` of two or more rows on such a model could then raise a database error.

The UNNEST path ignores per-field placeholders (`get_placeholder`) and any custom `db_type` handling, such as GIS geometry fields (`ST_GeomFromEWKB(%s)`). PostGIS inherits this compiler through `compiler_module`. A bulk insert of geometry values or other fields that need special placeholders is rewritten to `(%s)::geometry(...)[]`, binding adapter objects as an array, and that likely fails or gives wrong results. The eligibility check only excludes `as_sql` values and array types, not fields with custom placeholders.

_create_alternatives now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`, which breaks any code that adds plain tuples to `msg.alternatives` directly. For example, `msg.alternatives.append((html, 'text/html'))` or `msg.alternatives = [(html, 'text/html')]` would previously work, but now `message()` raises AttributeError. Only `__init__` and `attach_alternative` wrap values in the `Alternative` namedtuple, so direct assignment and mutation bypass it.

`_create_alternatives` now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`. Code that appends plain `(content, mimetype)` tuples directly to `msg.alternatives` used to work, because the old code unpacked with `*alternative`. It now raises AttributeError at send or `message()` time. `__init__` converts tuples, but direct mutation of the list is not covered, so this is a backward-compatibility regression for existing users.

The `single_object` keyword argument is removed from the public `log_actions()` signature. Any caller written against the 5.1 API (for example `log_actions(..., single_object=True)`) now raises `TypeError`, and the change adds no deprecation or compatibility shim. Return behavior also becomes implicit: a one-element queryset returns a single `LogEntry`, while any other length returns a list from `bulk_create`. This is the intended design, and `log_actions` was only introduced in 5.1, so the practical impact is probably small.

GenericIPAddressField.to_python passes self.max_length straight to clean_ipv6_address. A user who explicitly passes max_length=None (valid for CharField, and previously accepted here) now hits `len(ip_str) > None` in _ipv6_address_from_str. For any value containing ':' this raises TypeError instead of validating or raising ValidationError. setdefault does not replace an explicit None.

Passing `max_length=None` explicitly to the form `GenericIPAddressField` is allowed, because `setdefault` keeps the explicit None. `to_python` then calls `clean_ipv6_address(..., max_length=None)` for any value containing ':'. That reaches `len(ip_str) > None` in `_ipv6_address_from_str`, which raises TypeError instead of a ValidationError or a successful clean. This previously worked, since the form field had no max_length default.

The SelectBox cache guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` (the select that triggered the popup) rather than the cache of the select being updated (`select.id`). When the popup was opened from a filter_horizontal/vertical M2M widget, `currentSelect` is the `_to` select, which has a cache entry. The guard is then false, and other M2M available-source selects for the same model get the option added to the DOM but not to their SelectBox cache. The next redisplay, such as a filter keystroke or a move, drops the new option or loses sync. In the FK case, `cache[currentSelect.id]` is undefined, so the branch always runs and calls `add_to_cache` on any available-source select whose cache is missing. That would throw a TypeError.

The SelectBox cache guard checks `currentSelect.id` but the cache update is applied to `select.id`. When the popup was opened from a plain select, `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` is undefined, so the branch runs for every related select. `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, ...)` then throws a TypeError for any related select that isn't a SelectBox, because its cache entry is undefined. When the popup was opened from a filter_horizontal "to" box, which does have a cache, the branch never runs. Other filter widgets for the same model are then updated in the DOM but not in their cache, so the new option disappears on the next redisplay or filter. The check should be on `select.id`. The option is also already added to `select.options`, so a cached widget would show it twice.

The `%d` interpolation is applied to the msgid strings before they reach `ngettext` (`"...%d character." % self.min_length`). The lookup keys become e.g. "...at least 8 character.", which don't exist in any translation catalog. The original msgids with `%(min_length)d` therefore never match, and the too-short error is always shown in English, even for locales that have translations. It also generates a different msgid for every `min_length`, and makemessages would no longer extract the original strings. The interpolation should be done on the result of `ngettext`.

The `params={"min_length": self.min_length}` argument was dropped from the `ValidationError`. Code that reads `error.params['min_length']` now gets `None`. Subclass overrides of `get_error_message()` that return a `%(min_length)d` placeholder will not be interpolated. This is a backward-compatibility regression, and it is inconsistent with the other validators, which still pass params.

`get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to the msgid strings before passing them to `ngettext`. The msgids become e.g. "...at least 8 characters.", which no longer match the catalog entries (those use `%(min_length)d`). Translations for the too-short error therefore silently stop working and the message is always English. The original code translated first and interpolated afterwards.

`ValidationError` no longer receives `params={"min_length": self.min_length}`, which is a regression. Code that inspects `error.params` (custom form or API error handling) loses `min_length`. Subclass overrides of `get_error_message()` that use `%(min_length)d`, as with the other validators' `%(verbose_name)s` placeholder, are not interpolated and display the raw placeholder.

`pre_migrate.connect` is called without a `sender`. `emit_pre_migrate_signal` fires once per app config with the same `plan`, so `rename_permissions` runs once per installed app. Each run inserts another `RenamePermission` after every `RenameModel`, leaving N duplicate operations. The duplicates are wasteful and redo the rename. The `assertOperationsInjected` test only checks the next operation, so it would not catch this. The handler should be connected with `sender=self`.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, a substring match. Renaming `Foo` also selects content types and permissions of unrelated models such as `foobar` or `myfoo` in the same app. Those permissions are then renamed to `*_<newmodel>`, which corrupts them. It should be an exact match on `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is rewritten using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix and a generated name. Custom permissions such as `can_export_oldmodel` or `publish_article` become `can_newmodel` or `publish_newmodel`, losing their meaning. Several custom permissions can also collapse to the same codename. The code never checks that a codename actually has the `<action>_<oldmodel>` form, and the generated name replaces any custom permission names.

`Permission.objects` is used without `.using(db)`. When migrating a non-default database, the live Permission model reads and writes the router's default database instead of `schema_editor.connection.alias`. The `ContentType` lookup from the frozen apps uses the migration's connection, so the two queries can hit different databases. `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=ctypes.values('id'))` also builds a subquery that may span databases.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match rather than an exact match. Renaming `User` to `Customer` in an app that also has `UserProfile` or `SuperUser` selects those models' content types too. Their permissions are then rewritten to `*_customer` with the wrong names, which corrupts unrelated permissions. The lookup should be `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the matching content type is rewritten to `<prefix>_<newmodel>`, where the prefix is whatever precedes the first underscore in the codename. Custom permissions such as `publish_article` or `can_do_something` get renamed to `publish_newmodel` and receive the generated name `Can publish new model`. This destroys custom permissions and breaks any code that checks the original codename. Prefixes containing underscores are also truncated.

`permission.save()` is called without `using=db`, and the `Permission.objects.filter(...)` and `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` queries also ignore the migration's database alias. The `transaction.atomic(using=db)` block uses the target database while the save goes through the router's default write database. With `migrate --database=other` or a multi-database setup, permissions in the wrong database are read or modified. The atomic block then does not protect the save, so an IntegrityError can break the target connection's transaction.

The new MRO scan collects every property found in any class's __dict__ and never checks whether a more-derived class shadows that name with a non-property. The old code used getattr_static, which respected MRO precedence. If a base class defines a property and a subclass overrides it with a plain attribute, method, or model field, the name is still reported as a property. This regression can affect Model.__init__ kwargs handling and the get_or_create/update_or_create parameter checks, which may then treat a non-property as a settable property. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

The new implementation takes the union of every property found in any class's __dict__ across the MRO. It ignores shadowing: if a parent defines a property and a subclass overrides that name with a non-property (a model field, plain attribute, or None), the name is still reported as a property. The old getattr_static approach resolved the name through the MRO and would have excluded it. Callers of _property_names (Model.__init__ kwargs handling, and get_or_create/update_or_create param filtering) can then misclassify the field as a read-only property. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

The check `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` compares Field instances. Field.__eq__ uses creation_counter and model, so two separate instances of the same field class are never equal. Any Subquery given an explicit output_field, for example `output_field=IntegerField()`, therefore gets wrapped in an ExpressionWrapper even when the type matches the query's own output field. That wrapper defeats the stated goal of exposing a plain Query as the lookup's right-hand side. Composite-pk tuple lookups that test `isinstance(rhs, Query)`, including the new NotSupportedError check, would then not recognise these subqueries. The comparison should be on field type, not instance equality.

resolve_expression reads `self.output_field` and only catches AttributeError. When the subquery's output field cannot be determined (for example a values() query with several columns, or a queryset with no single select column), BaseExpression.output_field raises FieldError, not AttributeError. The error would now surface eagerly at resolve time instead of lazily, and the intended fallback of returning `resolved.query` would be skipped. Previously working subqueries, such as multi-column `__in` subqueries, could crash.
